topic.name: Line Integrals of Scalar Functions Over Polar Curves

question.text: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq 0.$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta = 2\cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta = 2\sin\theta. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\cos\theta$ and $y=2\sin\theta$, where $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq 0.$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x+y$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= 2\cos\theta + 2\sin\theta \\[5pt] &= 2(\cos\theta + \sin\theta). \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left( 2 \right) = 0, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{ 2^2 + 0^2} \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C}(x+y)\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{-\pi/4}^{0} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{-\pi/4}^{0} 2(\cos\theta + \sin\theta) \cdot 2 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= 4\int_{-\pi/4}^{0} (\cos\theta + \sin\theta) \,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= 4 (\sin\theta - \cos\theta) \Bigg|_{-\pi/4}^{0} \\[5pt] &= 4 \left( [0 - 1] - \left[-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right] \right) \\[5pt] &= 4(\sqrt{2} - 1) \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ along the polar curve $r=2\, $ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4} .$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta =2 \cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta = 2\sin\theta . \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=2 \cos\theta $ and $y= 2\sin\theta $, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2-y^2$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= (2\cos \theta )^2 - (2\sin \theta)^2 \\[5pt] &=4\cos ^2\theta -4 \sin^2\theta\\[5pt] &=4\left(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta\right)\\[5pt] &= 4\cos2\theta. \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left(2 \right) = 0, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{ 2^2 + 0^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{4} \\[5pt] &=2. \end{align*}

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C}(x^2-y^2)\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{0}^{\pi/4} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 4\cos 2\theta \cdot 2 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 8\cos 2\theta \, \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= 4 \sin2\theta\, \Biggr|_{0}^{\pi/4} \\[5pt] &= 4(\sin(\pi/2)-\sin 0) \\[5pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Given in Polar Form

question.text: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ along the polar curve $r=\sin\theta\, $ for $\dfrac\pi 4 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} .$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin \theta\cdot \cos\theta \\[5pt] &=\sin \theta \cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin\theta\sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin^2\theta. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sin \theta \cos\theta $ and $y= \sin^2\theta $, where $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y) =\sqrt{ x^2+y^2}$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= \sqrt{(\sin \theta \cos\theta)^2 + (\sin^2 \theta)^2} \\[5pt] &=\sqrt{\sin ^2\theta \cos^2\theta+\sin^4\theta}\\[5pt] &=\sqrt{\sin^2\theta\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\right)}\\[5pt] &=\sqrt{ \sin^2\theta}\\[5pt] &= |\sin \theta|\\[5pt] &= \sin\theta. \end{align*}

Notice that $ |\sin \theta|= \sin\theta$ because $ \dfrac\pi 4 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \quad \Longrightarrow\quad \sin\theta > 0.$

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left(\sin\theta \right) = \cos\theta, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{ (\sin\theta)^2 + (\cos\theta)^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{1} \\[5pt] &=1. \end{align*}

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{\pi/ 4}^{\pi/2} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \sin\theta \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \sin\theta\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= -\cos\theta\Biggr|_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= -0-\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt2}2\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sqrt2}2 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Given in Polar Form

question.text: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=6$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta = 6\cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta = 6\sin\theta. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=6\cos\theta$ and $y=6\sin\theta$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y) = xy$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= 6\cos\theta\cdot 6\sin\theta \\[5pt] &= 36\cos\theta \sin\theta. \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left( 6 \right) = 0, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{ 6^2 + 0^2} \\[5pt] &= 6. \end{align*}

We can now write the integral as

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C} xy \,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{0}^{\pi/3} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/3} 36\cos\theta \sin\theta \cdot 6 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= 6\int_{0}^{\pi/3} 6\cos\theta \cdot 6\sin\theta \,\textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\sin\theta,$ $\textrm d u=6\cos\theta\,\textrm d\theta$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 6\int_{0}^{\pi/3} 6\cos\theta \cdot 6\sin\theta \,\textrm{d}\theta &= 6 \int_0^{3\sqrt{3}} u \, \text{d}u \\[5pt] &= 6\cdot \dfrac 1 2 u^2 \bigg|_0^{3\sqrt{3}} \\[5pt] &= 3\left(\left(3\sqrt 3\right)^2 - 0^2\right) \\[5pt] &= 3\cdot 27 \\[5pt] &= 81 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Using Substitution

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{x^4}{y^2} \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r = \tan{\theta}\:$ for $\dfrac \pi 6 \le \theta \le \dfrac \pi 3?$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \tan{\theta} \cdot \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} \cdot \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \tan{\theta} \cdot \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} \cdot \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sin^2 \theta}{\cos \theta}. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sin{\theta}$ and $y=\dfrac{\sin^2{\theta}}{\cos\theta}$, where $\dfrac \pi 6 \le \theta \le \dfrac \pi 3.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^4}{y^2}$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= \dfrac{\sin^4 \theta}{\left( \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \cos^2\theta. \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left( \tan{\theta} \right) = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 \theta}, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{\left( \tan{\theta} \right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 \theta} \right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{ \dfrac{\sin^2{\theta}}{\cos^2 \theta} + \dfrac{1}{\cos^4 \theta} } \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{ \dfrac{\sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta + 1}{\cos^4\theta} } \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sqrt{ \sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta + 1}}{\cos^2\theta}. \end{align*}

Finally, we can write the integral as

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C} \dfrac{x^4}{y^2} \,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \cos^2\theta \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{ \sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta + 1}}{\cos^2\theta} \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \sqrt{ \sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta + 1} \,\textrm{d}\theta . \end{align*}
